summary: Explains why the Stringprep approach, used by IDNA2003 and several protocol profiles, needs revision, and states the problem for a new framework called PRECIS for preparing and comparing internationalized strings. It is a problem statement, and it is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers must tell whether two names are the same even when written with fancy letters. This explains why the old way of cleaning up names fell short and what a new way must do.

questions: what is the difference between idna2003 and idna2008
subtitle: Why the old Stringprep approach to comparing international text needed replacing, and what a successor had to handle.

tldr.problem: Many protocols use Stringprep profiles to prepare Unicode strings (usernames, names, passwords) so they can be compared, but Stringprep is tied to Unicode 3.2 and has other limits.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC is a problem statement: it lists the limits of Stringprep profiles, the questions any replacement must answer, and guidance for designing one that works more like IDNA2008.
tldr.outcome: It defines no protocol. It set out the work for the PRECIS working group and is informational.

today: RFC 6885 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It states the problem only; it does not define the replacement itself.

sections.title: Introduction: Stringprep and Its Users
sections.content:
If a protocol compares two strings and was built for ASCII only, then Unicode code points in those strings must be prepared somehow first. IDNA2003 defined Stringprep and the Nameprep profile for domain names (see RFC 3454, RFC 3490 and RFC 3491). Other protocols then defined their own Stringprep profiles, including iSCSI, XMPP, SASL, LDAP, EAP and NFSv4.

A review of these specifications found that they are very similar and fall into a small number of classes, and that many reuse the same profile, such as the SASL one. IDNA2003 was later replaced by IDNA2008, which does not use Stringprep or Nameprep at all. This document lists the problems found with Stringprep profiles and the requirements for a replacement.
sections.plainLanguage: Many programs clean up names the same old way before comparing them. One big user of that way, the web address system, has moved on, so the others need a new plan.

sections.title: Limits of Stringprep Profiles
sections.content:
A BOF at IETF 77 (March 2010) reached several conclusions. Stringprep is bound to Version 3.2 of Unicode and has not been updated, so protocols using it are stuck there. Applications usually cannot require Unicode 3.2 anyway, since they get whatever version the host provides. The protocols want the version agility of IDNA2008 and better bidirectional (bidi) support.

Backward compatibility matters if profiles change: Stringprep normalization may use NFKC, while IDNA2008 mostly uses NFC. Identifiers are also passed between protocols, so the same username may move between SASL, XMPP, LDAP and EAP, which favors a common set of rules or string classes.

The IESG formed the PRECIS working group to produce a replacement. The RFC cautions that IDNA2008 may be a poor model for other protocols, because it serves one very old protocol at the scale of the entire Internet and is deployed without changing DNS. Other protocols may be more local or have version negotiation built in.
sections.plainLanguage: The old cleaning rules only know about letters from one old dictionary, and nobody can keep that dictionary up to date. People want rules that keep working as new letters are added.

sections.title: Comparison and Types of Identifiers
sections.content:
Following an outside draft on identifier comparison, the RFC sorts identifiers into three classes by how they can be compared.

  • Absolute identifiers can be compared byte by byte for equality.
  • Definite identifiers have a well-defined comparison algorithm that all parties agree on, for example code points in different encodings that can be converted to one encoding.
  • Indefinite identifiers have no single algorithm that all parties agree on.

It is also necessary to evaluate what happens when a comparison gives a false positive or a false negative, especially for security and usability.
sections.plainLanguage: Some names match only if every letter is identical. Others match if both sides follow the same rulebook. Some have no shared rulebook at all, which is the tricky case.

sections.title: Dealing with Characters
sections.content:
The RFC lists the character-level questions a replacement has to settle.

  • Case: IDNA2003 maps labels to lowercase. IDNA2008 does no mapping; uppercase is simply not valid. If a protocol needs case preserved, the IDNA2008 analogy breaks down.
  • Normalization: most Stringprep profiles use NFKC, which is more aggressive than NFC at matching code points. That can be wrong for spelling of user names, but NFKC does handle character width, which can be crucial in practice.
  • Mapping and prohibited characters: some characters are mapped to others or to nothing, and some are simply disallowed. IDNA2008 is inclusion based: code points are disallowed unless Unicode properties show they are allowed, and some are allowed only in context, such as ZWJ (U+200D) and ZWNJ (U+200C).
  • Delimiters: characters such as full stop, commercial at, hyphen-minus, solidus and low line may have special meaning inside a protocol, and handling matters more than mere presence.
  • Homoglyphs: look-alike glyphs can enable phishing. IDNA2008 leaves this to zone operators, but a similar split may not suit every protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Capital letters, look-alike letters and special marks like dots and slashes all need clear rules, or two names that look the same could be treated as different, or the other way round.

sections.title: Guidance for a Stringprep Replacement
sections.content:
Section 5.3 adds questions about where strings come from and go: whether users type them, how they are displayed (a vCard versus the side of a bus), and whether they feed other operations such as hashing. It also asks how willing the community is to accept backward-incompatible changes, and notes that Unicode properties can change between versions, which has happened before.

The guidance in Section 6 is:

  • A Stringprep replacement should be defined.
  • It should work like IDNA2008, using properties of code points rather than whitelisting them.
  • Defining preparation for the smallest set of string classes may be enough for most cases.
  • It is reasonable to limit scope to Unicode code points and leave mapping from other character encodings out.
  • It ought to give guidance on handling incompatibilities caused by Unicode changes.
  • Compatibility between Stringprep-based techniques and the replacement must be considered very carefully.
sections.plainLanguage: The advice is to build one new, flexible rulebook for a few kinds of names, and to be careful not to break the programs that already use the old rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document defines no protocol, only states the problems to solve. It notes that the work to come will certainly have security implications, and that the Security Considerations of RFC 3454 still apply. The evaluations of existing profiles in Appendix B each carry their own analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper only lists problems, so it has no new rules to break. Safety questions come with the real solution later.

cells: Exclusion based: an explicit list of excluded or mapped-away characters; anything else in Unicode 3.2 is allowed
Inclusion based: code points are disallowed unless Unicode properties show they are allowed
